title: IVF: clustering the vector space
summary: Measured: at 256 cells, nearly half of queries have their nearest neighbour in a cell they did not pick, which is why nprobe is a correctness requirement rather than a tuning knob. Compared at equal work rather than equal nprobe, finer partitions win decisively, and the sqrt(N) rule falls out of balancing the coarse scan against the list scan.
html:
Three days of graphs. Today, the other family, which throws the graph away and goes back to something you have implemented a hundred times: partition the keyspace, look in the right partition.

The algorithm

Build time: run k-means over your vectors to get nlist centroids, then assign every vector to its nearest one. You now have nlist buckets, called inverted lists because the structure is the same inverted index from Day 3 with centroids instead of terms.

Query time: compare the query against the nlist centroids, take the nprobe nearest, scan only those lists.

build:  centroids = kmeans(X, nlist)
        lists[c] = [i for i where nearest_centroid(X[i]) == c]

query:  cells = top_nprobe(query . centroids)
        candidates = concat(lists[c] for c in cells)
        return top_k(query . X[candidates])

That is the whole index. No graph, no insertion order dependence, no diversity heuristic. Compared to the ninety lines of Day 19 it is about fifteen.

The problem this family has

Partitioning assumes the answer is in the partition you picked. Here is how often that holds. I measured, for each query, whether its true nearest neighbour lives in the single cell the query routes to:

nlist=  16   nearest neighbour in the query's own cell:  75.7%
nlist=  64                                               65.0%
nlist= 256                                               56.3%
nlist=1024                                               57.3%

At 256 cells, nearly half of all queries have their best answer in a cell they did not pick. The query and its nearest neighbour sit on opposite sides of a Voronoi boundary. Nothing is wrong with the clustering. In high dimensions almost everything is near a boundary, so this is structural.

That is what nprobe exists for, and why it is not a tuning nicety but a correctness requirement. nprobe=1 is not a fast configuration of IVF, it is a broken one.

Contrast with Day 17's graph, which has no boundaries at all. A walk crosses whatever region it needs to. Partitioning buys simplicity and pays for it with edges that are not there.

Choosing nlist, and a comparison that lies

Read my first table at fixed nprobe and you would conclude fewer cells is better:

at nprobe=4:   nlist=16 -> 0.951     nlist=256 -> 0.754

That comparison is meaningless. With 16 cells each list holds 388 vectors, with 256 it holds 24, so the first configuration is scanning sixteen times as much data. Of course it wins.

Compare at equal work instead, which is fraction of the corpus actually scanned:

  ~6.6% scanned:  nlist=16, nprobe=1  -> 0.730
                  nlist=64, nprobe=4  -> 0.873
                  nlist=256, nprobe=16 -> 0.934

 ~13.0% scanned:  nlist=16, nprobe=2  -> 0.869
                  nlist=64, nprobe=8  -> 0.949
                  nlist=256, nprobe=32 -> 0.974

The ordering inverts completely. Finer partitions dominate at equal work, and by a lot: 0.934 against 0.730 for the same bytes read. More cells means more boundary misses, and it also means each probe is cheap enough to afford many of them, and the second effect wins.

The general habit here is worth more than the result. When you compare two configurations of anything that trades work for quality, hold the work fixed. Comparing at fixed parameter is how you talk yourself into the wrong setting.

So why not a million cells

Because the coarse quantizer is itself a linear scan. Every query compares against all nlist centroids before it looks at a single data vector. Counting total vector comparisons per query on my 6,200 vectors at nprobe=8:

 nlist   coarse   list scan    total   coarse share
    16       16        3100     3116             1%
    64       64         775      839             8%
   256      256         194      450            57%
  1024     1024          48     1072            95%

At 1,024 cells, 95 percent of the work is deciding which cells to read. You have rebuilt the problem from Day 15 one level up, and the index is now mostly overhead.

That tension has a clean solution. Set nlist to roughly the square root of N. Then there are sqrt(N) centroids and each list holds sqrt(N) vectors, so the coarse scan and the list scan are the same size and both grow as sqrt(N) rather than N. The usual advice to use sqrt(N) is not folklore, it is the point where the two halves balance.

N =      10,000  ->    100 centroids,    100 vectors per list
N =   1,000,000  ->  1,000 centroids,  1,000 vectors per list
N = 100,000,000  -> 10,000 centroids, 10,000 vectors per list

Memory is cheap by comparison: at sqrt(N) the centroids plus one list id per vector come to a couple of percent on top of the raw vectors, against HNSW's edges at eight percent and climbing.

Why this family survives

On recall per unit of work in RAM, a good graph index generally beats IVF. The reason IVF is still everywhere is the access pattern, and it is the part that should interest you most.

A graph search is pointer chasing. Each hop reads a neighbour list, picks one, jumps somewhere unrelated, reads again. That is random access with no locality, which is why Day 15's bandwidth argument bites so hard and why HNSW effectively has to live in RAM. Put it on SSD and every hop is a separate round trip.

An IVF list is a contiguous run of vectors. You decide which lists you want, then read each one start to finish. That is nprobe large sequential reads, which is exactly the access pattern storage is built for: readahead works, queue depth works, and you can keep the vectors on disk and only the centroids in memory.

So the families split by where your data lives. Fits in RAM: use a graph. Does not: use cells, because sequential reads of the right regions beat random reads of the right vectors by more than the recall difference costs you. Day 25 is DiskANN, which is what happens when someone takes that observation seriously and builds a graph that respects it anyway.

IVF also still stores full vectors, so a billion of them is still 1.5 TB. Tomorrow starts fixing that: product quantization, and how to make a vector 24 times smaller and still compute distances against it.
exercise:
1. Measure your own boundary rate. Cluster your embeddings into sqrt(N) cells. For each held-out query, check whether its true nearest neighbour sits in the single cell the query routes to. The percentage you get is the floor on what nprobe=1 can ever achieve, and it is lower than most people guess.

2. Build the honest comparison. For two or three values of nlist, plot recall against fraction of corpus scanned rather than against nprobe. Confirm the curves reorder when you switch the x axis. If you only ever make one plot about an index, make this one.

3. Find where the coarse scan takes over. For your N and your nprobe, compute nlist versus nprobe * N / nlist and find the nlist where the first exceeds the second. Past that point you are paying more to choose cells than to search them, and no amount of nprobe tuning helps.
